A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VAP research work. All pages, including figures, tables, equations, and appendices, support comparison; retained content can be matched across rewriting and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulation and physical-robot experiments in Tables 2–4 and Figure 5, plus embedding, attention, and failure analyses.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds component ablations in Tables 10–13 and a real-world sequential manipulation experiment in Table 14.

M1.justification: The core grounding, tracking, highlighting, and instruction-rewriting pipeline remains. Appendix F adds sequential execution of compound requests: decompose into sub-goals, manipulate one target, clear its mask, and re-ground the next target after the scene changes. The cross-view association proposal in Appendix D.2 remains future work.

E1.justification: The main simulation benchmarks and generic training tasks remain. The real-world suite replaces the marker task with a pouch task, confirmed by descriptions and images. Appendix F adds a limited shared-scene scenario requiring sequential manipulation of two users' objects, a dog figurine and an ornament.

E2.justification: The main Generic VLA, Soft Prompt, and Short/Long Hard Prompt comparator families remain. New Appendix E adds controlled comparison variants against full VAP: Mask-only, Rewrite-only, averaging instead of voting, and bounding-box prompting.

E3.justification: Table 4 changes stated VLABench episodes per task/run from 25 to 50, although Table 9 retains 125×10 total episodes. Appendix A changes the reported real-world action horizon from 4 to 32 and hard-prompt generation from GPT-4o with one reference view to GPT-5.1 with all views. New ablations introduce reference-count, opacity, and component controls; Appendix F adds a 20-trial two-step protocol and metrics. These reporting revisions do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V1 includes token-embedding, attention, and failure analyses but lacks the component ablations added in Appendix E. Tables 10–13 test highlight/rewrite coupling, voting versus averaging, reference counts, and prompt geometry/opacity. V2 also revises attention examples and adds real-world success and failure rollouts, substantially expanding diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: Figure 5 newly includes error bars identified as standard deviations across four tasks. Tables 3–4 explicitly identify their reported values as means; both versions already state ten runs. The added variability reporting concerns differences across tasks and does not establish additional seeds, confidence intervals, or increased repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: Table 2 changes VAP's bottle visual-matching CMR/SR from 73.2/60.6 to 83.2/75.0 and variant-aggregation SR from 58.2 to 62.5. Figure 5 replaces marker results with pouch results and changes mean pick-and-place SR from 56.2 to 58.8; revised tasks/settings prevent treating this as a matched performance gain. Tables 10–14 add substantial ablation and sequential-task results, including 65.0% two-step success.

T1.justification: Appendix D.2 adds mathematical definitions for shared cross-view assignments, including an unobserved-target option, and a MAP-style objective combining reference evidence, cross-view consistency, and visibility priors. It also defines alternative association scores and geometric penalties. This is a localized formalization of future work; the existing grounding equations remain and no proofs or guarantees are added.

C1.justification: The principal claims about training-free personalization of frozen VLAs and superiority over prompting baselines remain. The introduction newly claims that the visual highlight and matched instruction rewrite must work together, with neither component alone reliably closing the control gap, sharpening the claimed contribution beyond the earlier effectiveness claim.

C2.justification: Appendix E adds interpretations concerning language–vision alignment, reference consensus, reference-count saturation, and the saliency–occlusion tradeoff. Expanded Appendix D.2 explains why reference voting cannot enforce cross-camera identity and discusses risks of erroneous joint associations. Appendix F qualifies the multi-user demonstration as reference-based ownership binding rather than visual ownership inference. These substantially expand mechanism and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies reference cropping, normalized final-layer DINOv2 CLS features, voting tie-breaking, missing-detection/mask fallbacks, and default opacity 0.5. It expands rewriting and sequential-execution instructions, adds a project-page link, and identifies a commit for the referenced π0 implementation. These improve implementation specificity without establishing changes to the core perception procedure.

R1.justification: Section 2 removes the Octo and GR00T N1.5 citations while retaining the broad positioning against foundation-model personalization and visual prompting. Appendix A.3 adds a connection to identifier conventions in DreamBooth and Yo’LLaVA. Most other reference changes update metadata or convert existing footnotes into bibliography entries.

P1.justification: Large portions of the introduction, related work, method overview, benchmark descriptions, results, and conclusion are rewritten and condensed. V2 adds an instruction-rewriting subsection and separate ablation and practical-usage appendices, while moving the existing discussion from Appendix E to G. The extensive editing goes beyond inserting new scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 adds Tables 10–14, real-world rollout Figures 18–20, and the sequential demonstration in Figure 24. Existing failure figures are renumbered, with real-world examples added to two of them. Attention Figures 9–12 are revised, and Figure 5 gains error bars and updated task imagery. Main-text tables and figures also move within the condensed layout.

improvement.justification: V1 demonstrates effectiveness but does not isolate the contributions of VAP's components. V2's Tables 10–13 address this important validation gap through controlled comparisons and sensitivity tests, substantially strengthening support for the design. Additional implementation details and applicability analysis also help. Reporting remains imperfect: Table 9's VLABench episode count conflicts with revised Table 4, and its unchanged 31.9% real-world failure rate conflicts with Figure 5's updated scores, which imply about 30.6%. These issues temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial validation gains.
